Module 4 | Beginner study guide

Linear Text Classification

Understand three ways to sort text: logistic regression gives probabilities, the perceptron learns by correcting mistakes, and an SVM looks for the widest safety margin.

Plain-language explanations + real-world examples + memory cues

Start with the big picture

A text classifier takes a message, turns it into numbers, and uses those numbers to choose a category. M4 studies three linear classifiers that share one basic calculation but learn and interpret it differently.

Real-world example: sorting a support inbox. A help desk might label messages as billing or technical support. Words such as “refund” may push a message toward billing; “screen frozen” may push it toward technical support. The model learns which clues matter from labeled examples.

Three memory hooks: logistic regression asks “how likely?”, perceptron asks “which side?”, and SVM asks “which boundary leaves the biggest cushion?”

Represent text Linear score Logistic regression Perceptron SVM Compare models Self-check

1. First turn text into numbers

Computers cannot directly calculate with a sentence, so we represent its words with numeric features. Two common choices in the course are:

Bag of Words

Counts or marks words from a vocabulary. It records which words occur, but mostly ignores their order.

Example: “refund delayed refund” gives the word refund a larger count than delayed.

TF-IDF

Weights words by how useful they are for distinguishing documents. Common words often get less weight than informative ones.

Example: “the” is less distinctive than “overheating” in a product complaint.

After vectorization, a document might be represented as x = [0.0, 0.7, 0.2, ...]. Each position corresponds to a feature, such as a vocabulary term. The vector can have thousands of dimensions, even though diagrams often show only two.

Keep the pipeline consistent: Fit the text vectorizer using training documents, then use that same fitted vectorizer to transform new and test documents. Otherwise, the model may receive features in a different vocabulary or order.

2. A shared idea: the linear score

All three models can begin with a weighted score:

score = f(x) = w · x + b
  • x is the document's feature vector.
  • w contains learned weights—one importance value per feature.
  • b is a bias or intercept that shifts the boundary.
  • w · x is the dot product: multiply corresponding numbers and add them.

Suppose a spam model gives “free prize” a positive weight and “meeting agenda” a negative weight. The words present in an email push its score in one direction or the other. The classifier then interprets that score according to its own rules.

The decision boundary

The line where the score equals zero separates the two predictions: w · x + b = 0. With two features it is a line; with three it is a plane; with many text features it is called a hyperplane. “Linear” describes this boundary in the feature space—even when the original text is complicated.

Linear separability means one such flat boundary can separate every example of one class from every example of the other. Real-world messages can overlap and contain noise, so perfect separation is not always possible.

3. Logistic regression: “How likely is it?”

A raw linear score can be any real number. Logistic regression passes it through the sigmoid function, which squeezes it into a value from 0 to 1:

sigmoid(s) = 1 / (1 + e−s)

The output is treated as the estimated probability of the positive class. A score of zero becomes probability 0.5; a strongly positive score moves toward 1, and a strongly negative score moves toward 0.

Example: customer feedback. A review classifier estimates a 0.82 probability that feedback is positive. A business can use that probability to decide which reviews need human attention, rather than receiving only an unexplained “positive” label.

From probability to a label

A common default is to predict positive when the probability is at least 0.5. But 0.5 is a choice, not a law. If missing a safety complaint is costly, a system might lower the threshold to catch more possible complaints, accepting that more ordinary messages will also be flagged.

Changing the threshold changes the operating point without retraining the model. ROC curves and AUC help compare classifier performance over different thresholds.

How does it learn?

The model compares its predicted probabilities with the correct training labels using a likelihood-based objective, often expressed as log loss. It adjusts weights to make correct predictions more likely. There is usually no simple closed-form answer for the weights, so an optimizer such as gradient descent updates them step by step.

Gradient descent analogy: imagine walking downhill in fog. The gradient estimates the direction of steepest increase in error, so the optimizer steps in the opposite direction. The step size is the learning rate: too big can overshoot; too small can make learning slow.

Memory cue: Logistic regression = linear score → sigmoid → probability.

Despite its name, logistic regression is commonly used for classification. Its standard decision boundary is linear in the chosen features.

4. Perceptron: learn by correcting mistakes

The perceptron is a simple hard classifier. It uses the sign of the score: one side means positive, the other negative. Unlike logistic regression, it does not directly return a probability.

Example: quick spam sorting. If an email falls on the model's “spam” side, the perceptron calls it spam. If a labeled spam email lands on the non-spam side, the training algorithm adjusts the weights so that this example is more likely to be placed correctly next time.

The update idea

During training, the perceptron looks at examples one by one. If a document is misclassified, it moves the weights toward the correct label. For labels y = −1 or +1, a common update is:

if y × score ≤ 0: update weights in the direction y × x

Repeat this process over the training data. If the data are linearly separable, the standard perceptron can find a separating boundary. If they are not, it may keep making changes without settling, so implementations set a maximum number of passes (epochs).

Important: the perceptron can stop at any boundary that works on separable training data. It does not try to find the most robust or widest-margin boundary, and the chosen solution can depend on the order examples are presented.

Memory cue: Perceptron = guess a side; when wrong, nudge the boundary.

5. SVM: leave the biggest possible cushion

A Support Vector Machine (SVM) also finds a decision boundary, but it does not settle for just any separating line. It aims to maximize the margin—the space between the boundary and the closest training examples.

Everyday analogy: a road between two neighborhoods. If one group of homes is on each side of a road, a wider road provides more buffer. Small shifts or noisy measurements are less likely to put a home on the wrong side. SVM looks for this widest buffer between classes.

Support vectors

The closest examples to the boundary are called support vectors. They strongly influence where the SVM places its margin. Far-away examples are less important to the boundary than these edge cases.

For the idealized hard-margin case, labels are often written −1 and +1, and the closest examples sit on margin boundaries at score −1 and +1. The decision boundary is at score zero. The total margin width is 2 / ||w||, so maximizing the margin corresponds to minimizing the weight-vector length while respecting the margin constraints.

Real data: soft margins and C

Text categories often overlap; for instance, a message can discuss both billing and a technical problem. A soft-margin SVM allows some examples inside the margin or even on the wrong side.

  • Large C: penalizes margin violations more strongly and prioritizes fitting training examples.
  • Small C: tolerates more violations in exchange for a wider, more regularized margin.

Kernel trick: a curved boundary without drawing all the curves

If a straight line cannot separate the data, a kernel lets the SVM compare examples as if they had been mapped into a richer feature space. A straight boundary there can correspond to a curved boundary in the original space. The RBF kernel is one common choice.

Practical text tip: Linear SVMs are often a strong starting point for sparse, high-dimensional bag-of-words or TF-IDF features. Nonlinear kernels can be computationally expensive on large text datasets. SVM scores are not automatically calibrated probabilities.
Memory cue: SVM = choose the boundary with the widest cushion.

Perceptron“Which side is this on?”Hard classCorrects misclassified examplesBasic version may not converge on non-separable data

Need probabilities?

Logistic regression provides them directly. Threshold choice should reflect the cost of mistakes.

Want the simplest learning demo?

Perceptron makes the “learn from a mistake” update easy to visualize.

Want a strong text baseline?

Try a linear SVM with TF-IDF and evaluate it on held-out data.

These are starting points rather than rules. The best choice depends on the dataset, evaluation goal, and the consequences of false positives and false negatives.

7. A practical text-classification workflow

  1. Define labels: decide what categories mean and make examples consistent.
  2. Split examples: keep training data for learning and held-out validation/test data for evaluation.
  3. Vectorize text: fit Bag-of-Words or TF-IDF on training text; apply the same transformation to the held-out text.
  4. Train a baseline: compare models such as logistic regression, perceptron, and a linear SVM.
  5. Evaluate for the real goal: inspect accuracy and per-class precision/recall or a confusion matrix; do not rely on training accuracy alone.
  6. Adjust responsibly: tune thresholds, regularization, or kernels using validation data, then report a final score from a test set not used for tuning.
Real-world mistake costs differ: A spam filter may tolerate a few missed junk messages, but a fraud alert system may prioritize recall to catch more suspicious activity—even if it reviews more legitimate cases. Choose a threshold and metric based on the job, not a default number alone.

8. One-minute recap

  1. Text becomes numeric features such as Bag-of-Words or TF-IDF.
  2. The linear score is a weighted sum plus a bias.
  3. The perceptron uses a hard sign and updates when it makes a mistake.
  4. Logistic regression applies a sigmoid to produce a class probability.
  5. An SVM chooses a maximum-margin boundary shaped by its support vectors.
  6. Kernels can model nonlinear boundaries; soft margins handle overlap.
  7. Evaluate held-out examples and match your metrics and threshold to the real-world cost of errors.
Remember it in one breath: Perceptron corrects; logistic estimates probability; SVM widens the margin.

9. Quick self-check

Try answering before opening each explanation.

What does the linear score w · x + b represent?

It is a weighted sum of the document's numeric features plus a bias. It gives a raw score before the model decides whether to return a probability or a class.

Why does logistic regression produce a probability?

It applies a sigmoid function to the linear score, mapping any real-valued score to a number between 0 and 1.

Does a 0.5 classification threshold have to be used?

No. It is a common default. A different threshold may be more appropriate when false positives and false negatives have different costs.

What happens when the perceptron misclassifies a training example?

It adjusts its weights in the direction of that example's true label. The basic algorithm aims to find a separator, not the widest-margin separator.

What is a support vector?

It is a training example near or inside the SVM margin that helps determine the final boundary.

What does a larger SVM C value generally encourage?

It penalizes margin violations more strongly, placing more emphasis on fitting training examples and less on allowing a broad margin.

Why might an RBF kernel help with concentric circles?

A straight line cannot separate the circles in the original two-dimensional space. The kernel compares points as if in a richer feature space, which can produce a curved boundary back in the original space.

Which model should you choose if you need a probability without extra calibration?

Logistic regression directly returns probability estimates. Standard perceptrons and SVM decision scores are not probabilities.
